title: Turning an Action Into a Noun

sections.title: From verb to noun
sections.content: A verb tells you that something happens: *Los precios subieron*. A noun made from the verb turns the action into a thing: *la subida de los precios*. You can then use it as the subject of a new sentence and say nothing about who did it: *La subida de los precios preocupa a las familias*. Spanish has a few regular endings for these nouns, and the old subject or object of the verb follows with *de*.

sections.title: Verb clause and noun phrase
rows: la decisión de cerrar la tienda

sections.title: Common endings
rows: la llegada, la salida, la subida

items.spanish: La subida de los precios preocupa a muchas familias.
items.english: The rise in prices worries many families.

items.spanish: El aumento del tráfico molesta a los vecinos.
items.english: The increase in traffic bothers the neighbours.

items.spanish: La llegada del tren se anunció a las ocho.
items.english: The arrival of the train was announced at eight.

items.spanish: El cambio de horario sorprendió a todos.
items.english: The change of schedule surprised everyone.

sections.content: The noun keeps the idea of the verb but drops the doer. *Decidieron cerrar la tienda* says that someone decided; *la decisión de cerrar la tienda* does not. The gender comes with the ending: *la* subida, *el* aumento. In everyday talk the verb is often simpler, so use these nouns when a short, neutral sentence helps.
